title: I got tired of AI RPGs ignoring rules. So I built an open-source AI Gamemaster with a strict 2-Pass Engine
author: Ok_Mathematician2887
selftext:
Hey r/aigamedev,

Most generative AI games act as a "Yes, and..." improv partner. You type "I jump to the moon", and it just happens. No rules, no inventory, no challenge.

I wanted a real RPG experience, so I built **TaleWeaver**: A self-hosted Generative RPG Engine driven by an omniscient AI Gamemaster.

**How I solved "LLM Amnesia" (The 2-Pass Engine):**

The engine splits the workload to keep the game state intact:

1. **Pass 1 (Rule Engine):** Evaluates your action, checks stats, rolls virtual D20s, and outputs a strict JSON `GameEvent` to update HP or inventory.
2. **Pass 2 (The Director):** Translates that raw JSON outcome into atmospheric prose.

**Cinematic Audio & Narration:** I integrated Gemini 1.5 Flash TTS and ElevenLabs. The engine automatically parses director notes to build dramatic tension, making it feel like a high-budget audio drama.

**The Stack & Setup:**

* Python (FastAPI), Vue.js, SQLite, and Mermaid.js for dynamic mapping.
* Fully containerized 1-click Docker setup.
* **BYOK (Bring Your Own Key):** Uses LiteLLM. Cloud models are highly recommended for the complex JSON reasoning. Local Ollama is supported but currently experimental.

**Repo & Specs:**

[jschm42/taleweaver: A next-generation AI-powered text adventure engine featuring dynamic storytelling, procedural world-building, and immersive visual/auditory generation.](https://github.com/jschm42/taleweaver)

comments.author: HallucinatedGames
comments.body: This is cool! Thanks for sharing. I am interested myself in how can we embed LLM capabilities directly into the gaming experience. Creating NPC Dialog, Sidequests, etc. I am unsure what the right pick is - embed the LLM directly with some smaller models (Gemma 4 E2B example), which still eats up a ton of RAM, or do the callout to the frontier lab vendor or hosted service, but incur the costs and latency, etc. I guess time and experimentations will find the right paths forward. Exciting times.

replies.author: Ok_Mathematician2887
replies.body: Yes, that's a really fascinating topic. I've done a lot of experimenting with LLMs as Game Masters. It works best when you split the problem up. In the first pass, the LLM solely checks the ruleset and follows strict constraints. In the second pass, the story is driven forward. This is where the LLM is allowed to let loose a bit. That sometimes leads to incredibly thrilling narratives. And when you combine that with text-to-speech, you basically get a playable audiobook.

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body: Interesting, I have a similar but different system. Seems like this would only work well with a completely rigid gameplay system?  How would you deal with emergent situations that the game system doesn't account for?

replies.author: Ok_Mathematician2887
replies.body:
very good question. I made TaleWeaver actually a hybridd system. The AI acts as a "Smart Reference" that translates your creative actions into mechanics on the fly.

Instead of hardcoded rules for every situation, it uses a flexible "Game Event Schema". When something emergent happens, the AI interprets your intent and dynamically generates the appropriate stats, status effects, or world changes. It’s not about accounting for every situation in code, but giving the AI a vocabulary to handle your creativity. This can generate very interesting interactions. In combination with NPCs that have their own goals and items in-game it feels quite alive. The AI ist realy good in playing the characters of all those NPCs. At least if you use the flagship models for the narrative.

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body: That's super cool, would definitelylike to learn more about thst. The problem as I see it is that flagship models can't work economically, at least not yet.   Players simply don't want to pay that much, regardless of quality.

replies.author: Ok_Mathematician2887
replies.body: True, they are very expensive. But there are models out there that work well for this, too. I am experimenting with DeepSeek-v4-Pro at the moment. It creates very nice narratives at a fraction of the cost. And I will test some more.

comments.author: MBernava
comments.body: The JSON retry logic on Pass 1 is the part that usually kills latency in practice — what's your fallback when the model hallucinates outside the schema? Do you re-prompt, repair, or abort the turn?

replies.author: Ok_Mathematician2887
replies.body: I do abort and surface, no automatic re-prompt. There are some simple automatic repair mechanics, but if validation still fails after thar, the turn ist aborted immediately and an SSE is send to the frontend, which shows a "retry last action". But from my experience this happens rarely. for pass #1 I usually use chatgpt-5.4-mini. That works stable enough and has very good latency. So waiting times are quite short.
